title: Reading Scheme-like Expressions into Nested Lists
description: A tokenizer and recursive reader that parses parenthesized prefix expressions into Python lists, turning `(+ 1 (* 2 3))` into `['+', 1, ['*', 2, 3]]`.
source: draft: opencode free model + edit: codex

steps.description: `tokenize` inserts spaces around parentheses, then splits on whitespace. `(+ 1 (* 2 3))` becomes `['(', '+', '1', '(', '*', '2', '3', ')', ')']`.

`read` pops the first token. If it is `(` it builds a list by recursively calling `read` until it sees `)`, then pops the `)` and returns the list. This matches the grammar rule `datum -> ( datum* )`.
If the token is not `(` it tries `int(token)`. On success it returns the integer (matching `datum -> NUMBER`). On `ValueError` it returns the token as a string (matching `datum -> SYMBOL`).

steps.question: When `read` processes `['(', '+', '1', '(', '*', '2', '3', ')', ')']`, how many recursive calls to `read` happen, and what does each one return?
steps.answer: Three calls: the top call sees `(` and builds the outer list. A second call sees `+` and returns the string `'+'`. A third call sees `(` and builds the inner list `['*', 2, 3]`. The inner list's elements come from further recursive calls that return `'*'`, `2`, and `3`.

steps.description: Three test prints: `tokenize` shows the token list. `read` on the expression returns `['+', 1, ['*', 2, 3]]`. `read` on a bare `7` returns the integer `7`.
`read` processes the tokens. It pops `(`, enters the loop, reads `'+'` (string), `1` (int), then sees `(` and recurses to build `['*', 2, 3]`. Returns `['+', 1, ['*', 2, 3]]`.
`read(tokenize("7"))` returns the integer `7`. The single token is not `(` so it parses as an int.
